title: PDE Basics and Separation of Variables

blocks.x: A partial differential equation has an unknown function of two or more variables, and partial derivatives of it. For example $u(x,t)$ could be the temperature at position $x$ and time $t$. We write $u_t = \partial u/\partial t$, $u_{xx} = \partial^2u/\partial x^2$, and so on.
The order is the highest derivative. The PDE is linear if $u$ and its derivatives appear only to the first power and are not multiplied together. It is homogeneous if every term contains $u$.

rows: vibrating string, sound, waves in cables

blocks.x: Here $c$ is the wave speed and $k$ is the thermal diffusivity (units m$^2$/s).

Where they come from. Heat: the rate of change of heat in a small piece of rod equals the heat flowing in minus the heat flowing out. With Fourier’s law (flux proportional to $-u_x$) this gives $u_t = ku_{xx}$. Wave: Newton’s second law for a small piece of a string with tension $T$ and density $\rho$ gives $u_{tt} = (T/\rho)\,u_{xx}$, so $c^2 = T/\rho$. Laplace: the steady state of the heat equation has $u_t = 0$.
Take a rod with cross-section area $A$, density $\rho$, specific heat $c_p$ and thermal conductivity $\kappa$. Let $u(x,t)$ be the temperature. Consider the piece between $x$ and $x+\Delta x$.

Heat content: $\int_x^{x+\Delta x}\rho c_pu\,A\,\dd s$. Fourier’s law: heat flows from hot to cold, with flux (heat per area per time) $q = -\kappa u_x$. The heat entering through the left face per unit time is $Aq(x)$, and the heat leaving through the right face is $Aq(x+\Delta x)$. Energy balance:
\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\int_x^{x+\Delta x}\rho c_pu\,A\,\dd s = A\big[q(x) - q(x+\Delta x)\big] = A\kappa\big[u_x(x+\Delta x) - u_x(x)\big].
Divide by $A\Delta x$ and let $\Delta x\to0$. The left side tends to $\rho c_pu_t$ and the right side tends to $\kappa u_{xx}$:
u_t = k\,u_{xx},\qquad k = \frac{\kappa}{\rho c_p}.
An insulated end has no heat flux, $q = -\kappa u_x = 0$, so $u_x = 0$ there.

Take a string with tension $T$ and mass $\rho$ per unit length. Let $u(x,t)$ be the small vertical displacement. On the piece between $x$ and $x+\Delta x$, the tension pulls at both ends along the string. At a point where the string makes angle $\theta$ with the horizontal, the vertical component of the tension is $T\sin\theta\approx T\tan\theta = T\,u_x$ (for small slopes). The net vertical force on the piece is
T\big[u_x(x+\Delta x) - u_x(x)\big].
The mass of the piece is $\rho\Delta x$ and its acceleration is $u_{tt}$. By Newton’s second law,
\rho\,\Delta x\,u_{tt} = T\big[u_x(x+\Delta x) - u_x(x)\big].
Divide by $\Delta x$ and let $\Delta x\to0$: $\rho u_{tt} = Tu_{xx}$, that is
u_{tt} = c^2u_{xx},\qquad c^2 = \frac T\rho .
(The horizontal components $T\cos\theta\approx T$ cancel, so there is no horizontal motion at this order.)
For $A\,u_{xx} + B\,u_{xy} + C\,u_{yy} + (\text{lower-order terms}) = 0$, look at the sign of $B^2 - 4AC$:
$B^2 - 4AC < 0$: elliptic. Example: Laplace equation. Describes steady states.
$B^2 - 4AC = 0$: parabolic. Example: heat equation. Describes diffusion in time.
$B^2 - 4AC > 0$: hyperbolic. Example: wave equation. Describes waves with finite speed.

blocks.name: Derivation
blocks.title: Where the three types come from

blocks.x: Try new variables $\xi = \xi(x,y)$ in $Au_{xx} + Bu_{xy} + Cu_{yy} + \cdots = 0$. By the chain rule the coefficient of $u_{\xi\xi}$ in the new equation is $A\xi_x^2 + B\xi_x\xi_y + C\xi_y^2$. We would like to choose curves $\xi = \text{const}$ that make it zero, which simplifies the equation. Dividing by $\xi_y^2$ and writing $\lambda = \xi_x/\xi_y$:
A\lambda^2 + B\lambda + C = 0, \qquad \lambda = \frac{-B\pm\sqrt{B^2-4AC}}{2A}.

$B^2 - 4AC>0$: two real families of curves. We can remove both $u_{\xi\xi}$ and $u_{\eta\eta}$, leaving $u_{\xi\eta} + \cdots=0$. This is the form of the wave equation (see the d’Alembert derivation in Chapter 10). Hyperbolic.
$B^2 - 4AC = 0$: only one family. One second-derivative term remains, like $u_{\eta\eta} = \cdots$. This is the form of the heat equation. Parabolic.
$B^2 - 4AC<0$: no real curves. The best form is $u_{\xi\xi} + u_{\eta\eta}+\cdots=0$, the Laplace form. Elliptic.
The three types have different physical behaviour (waves with finite speed, diffusion, steady states), which is why we need different methods.
Wave $c^2u_{xx} - u_{tt} = 0$: $A = c^2$, $B=0$, $C=-1$, so $B^2 - 4AC = 4c^2>0$. Hyperbolic.
Heat $k\,u_{xx} - u_t = 0$: $A=k$, $B=C=0$, so $B^2-4AC=0$. Parabolic.
Laplace: $A=C=1$, $B=0$, so $-4<0$. Elliptic.
$x\,u_{xx} + u_{yy} = 0$: $B^2-4AC = -4x$. Elliptic for $x>0$, hyperbolic for $x<0$.

sections.title: Conditions that make the solution unique

blocks.x: A PDE alone has infinitely many solutions. We add conditions.
Boundary conditions (BC) on the edges of the region:
Dirichlet: the value of $u$ is given, e.g. $u(0,t)=0$ (end held at fixed temperature, or string fixed).
Neumann: the normal derivative is given, e.g. $u_x(0,t)=0$ (insulated end).
Robin: a mix of $u$ and $u_x$ (convective cooling at the end).
Initial conditions (IC) at $t=0$:
Heat equation: one condition, $u(x,0)=f(x)$.
Wave equation: two conditions, $u(x,0)=f(x)$ and $u_t(x,0)=g(x)$ (initial shape and initial velocity).
The Laplace equation has no time. It needs a boundary condition on the whole boundary.

If $u_1$ and $u_2$ solve a linear homogeneous PDE with linear homogeneous BCs, then so does $c_1u_1 + c_2u_2$, and so does an infinite sum $\sum c_nu_n$ (when it converges). We use this to build a solution from simple pieces.

blocks.name: Method
blocks.title: The standard recipe (for a rod or string on $0<x<L$)

blocks.x: Assume a product: $u(x,t) = X(x)\,T(t)$.
Put it in the PDE and divide so that all $x$ terms are on one side and all $t$ terms on the other. Both sides must equal a constant, which we call $-\lambda$.
This gives two ODEs: one for $X$ and one for $T$.
The homogeneous BCs on $X$ give an eigenvalue problem (Chapter 6). Solve it to get $\lambda_n$ and $X_n(x)$.
Solve the $T$ equation for each $\lambda_n$.
Superpose: $u = \sum_n X_n(x)T_n(t)$.
Fit the initial condition using a Fourier series (Chapter 7). This fixes the constants.

blocks.name: Derivation
blocks.title: Why the separation constant is a constant

blocks.x: After dividing by $kXT$ we have $\dfrac{T'(t)}{kT(t)} = \dfrac{X''(x)}{X(x)}$. The left side depends on $t$ only and the right side depends on $x$ only. Fix $t$ and vary $x$: the left side does not change, so the right side cannot change either. Hence both sides equal one constant, which we call $-\lambda$. (The minus sign is only a convenient notation. The boundary conditions will decide which values of $\lambda$ give non-zero solutions; see Chapter 6.) A product $X(x)T(t)$ is a very special type of solution, but sums of such products can fit any reasonable initial condition. That is the content of the Fourier series (Chapter 7).
$u_t = ku_{xx}$. Put $u = XT$: $XT' = kX''T$. Divide by $kXT$:
\frac{T'}{kT} = \frac{X''}{X} = -\lambda .
So we get two ODEs:
X'' + \lambda X = 0, \qquad T' + k\lambda\,T = 0 .
For the wave equation $u_{tt} = c^2u_{xx}$ the same steps give $X'' + \lambda X = 0$ and $T'' + c^2\lambda\,T = 0$.

Separation of variables works only if the PDE is linear and homogeneous, and the BCs are homogeneous ($u=0$ or $u_x=0$) on the sides where we build the eigenvalue problem. If the BCs are not homogeneous we first subtract a simple steady solution (see Chapter 11).
Classify $u_{xx} + 4u_{xy} + u_{yy} = 0$.
Classify $u_{xx} + 4u_{xy} + 4u_{yy} = 0$.
Classify $u_{xx} + 2u_{yy} = 0$.
Show that $u = \sin(\pi x)\,e^{-\pi^2kt}$ solves $u_t = ku_{xx}$.
Show that $u = \sin x\cos ct$ solves $u_{tt} = c^2u_{xx}$.
Apply separation of variables to $u_t = ku_{xx} - u$ and write the two ODEs.

(1) $B^2 - 4AC = 16 - 4 = 12 > 0$: hyperbolic.   (2) $16 - 16 = 0$: parabolic.   (3) $0 - 8 < 0$: elliptic.   (4) $u_t = -\pi^2k\,u$ and $u_{xx} = -\pi^2u$, so $ku_{xx} = -\pi^2k\,u$. ✓   (5) $u_{tt} = -c^2\sin x\cos ct$ and $c^2u_{xx} = -c^2\sin x\cos ct$. ✓   (6) $XT' = kX''T - XT$. Divide by $XT$: $T'/T + 1 = kX''/X = -k\lambda$, so $X'' + \lambda X = 0$ and $T' + (k\lambda + 1)T = 0$.
